What to know

  • Amino acids share a backbone. Each has an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen, and a side chain (R group) attached to the alpha carbon. The side chain sets charge, polarity, and size.
  • The peptide bond is planar. Condensation between the carboxyl of one amino acid and the amino group of the next releases water and gives a rigid, partial double bond.
  • Primary structure is the sequence. It is written N-terminus to C-terminus and is encoded by DNA. The sequence determines everything that follows.
  • Ionizable side chains buffer. Histidine, aspartate, glutamate, lysine, and arginine exchange protons near physiological pH and sit in enzyme active sites.
  • Disulfide bonds and chaperones. Cysteine pairs form covalent cross-links; chaperones help proteins fold and prevent aggregation.

Check

check.question: Which level of protein structure is the amino-acid sequence?
check.explanation: Primary structure is the linear order of amino acids. Secondary, tertiary, and quaternary structure describe local folding, the whole chain, and multi-subunit assembly.
